BEiRUT
Dear F
and F.,
Friday Dec. 4th, 1964.
We were invited to a very fine dinner last
night by a V-P of the Continental Oil Co. It was good to meet a
sizeable group of the American community. This morning Debby went
to the "SUQ" with some ladies she met at dinner.
"SUQ" is the
Arabic word for bazaar. She bought a bracelet and the next day,
Sat. Dec. 5th, she talked me into going around. You'd know that
you were not in Tiffany's. that evening we had dinner with the
Boyntons and the Bojonells, he is PAA #1 in Athens and was over here
on a brief business
trip.
We were glad to see them again. Boynton
had just come bask from Cyprus.
He said externally at least, Cyprus
never had it so good. Every hotel and cafe full every night with
free-spending United Nations people, Army officers and newspaper
reporters from all over the world.
Sun. Dec. 6th.
I have stayed in bed all day trying unsuccessfully
to shake a cold. Tomorrow we leave for Hong Kong. I feel a little
sad at not going to 8,000 foot level Teheran and some what lower
but colder Afghanastan as we had more or less planned. Guess I am
not tough like my old friend Phil Ball. No doubt most of you have
heard this story but a good story is always worth hepeating ( if you
don't do it too often).
Back in 1927 Mr. Ball bought a Ryan airplane
He asked me to recommend a pilot and I did. This particular man,
Frank Ryan Dunn, was about as homely and as tough as they come but
a good safe pilot.
When I sent Frank up to Mr. Ball's office for an
interview I said "Frank, make it perfectly clear right from the
start that Mr. Ball is boss on the ground bøt that you are boss in the
sky as well as deciding whether or not you should venture therein".
Frank went on upstairs and about 20 minutes later came back by my
desk in the old State National Bank. He said " Gee, I've met some
tough guys but we made a deal, we"ll get along all right". Another
five minutes and Mr. Ball came down "Say Bix, where in h---_ did
you find that porch climber?" They were together until Mr. Ball's
death (in bed) some 15 years later.
When the Ryan was ready for
delivery they went out to San Diego together.. Frank was checked
out on the plane and they took off for El Paso. Mr. Ball said
"Frank, climb up to 12,000 feet".
Frank demurred because it was a
slow climb with a full load but he went on up to 12,000 feet and
ran "down hill" into El Paso. As they were having dinner together
that night Frank said "Mr. Ball why did you want me to go to 12,000
feet?"
Mr. Ball said "Well Frank, I didn't want to worrys you
but
I don't mind telling you now. My doctor told me h*sth that if I
went up to 10,000 feet I'd drop dead. I knew that he didn't know
what he was talking about so I spotted him 2000 feet and as yau
know I'm still around".
Well I just do not have as much nerve as
old man Ball. When perhaps you can't get enough air to keep the
old pump going its better to play safe. I had another reason for
going to Teheran.
Years ago in New York, I got a call from a
White House contact asking me to meet a Mr. Pahlevi at theairport,
show him around, give him a good time, "quite important" Washington
said.
So I met Mr. Pahdevi who was a most friendly youngen,
We
went through the hangars, he tried the link trainer, and did quite
well, we had the usual buffet lunch where what you don't spill is
your own with a group of executives and piots and the young man
whose Oxford English was better tire

Bill Cowden, PAA#1 and George Sellett met us at the airport and escorted us
to the Intercontinental Mandarin, a 600 room 20 story hotel on Victoria
Post Office just behind the ferry landing.
Our room looks out on the harbor with its constantly changing seene of
ferry boats, there are & crossing as I write this line, hundreds of junks
freighters, from all over the world with a few war ships and a passenger
liner or two. Most of the freighters never touch shore, they are unloaded
and loaded by a swarn of small craft coming along side and leaving all day
and all night.
Wed. Dec. 9th•
We tended to tickets changing money etc. in the morning.
George Sellett came by for us about one o'clock and we drove to his house for
lunch.
We crossed to the mainland by auto ferry and then out Nathan road
by the old Peninsula Hotel and between apartment buildings, mostly new, to
the mountains that mark the beginning of the "leased territory". We climbed
up and up along a perfect road to the Carleton Hotel and just beyond that is
George's new "estate". We drove through a gate to find ourselves in a small
garden full of those wonderful chrysanthemums such as only Chinese gardeners
can grow.
The ground floor of the stone house is taken up with a screen
which partly hides a rumpus room which the former owner had for the .
children. A winding stairway leads to an upper floor with bedrooms, 3, each
with bath to the right and to the left a larger living room with roam high
sliğing glass doors which open on a wide terrace which overlooks the whold
of Hong Kong. From the terrace the land falls away steeply to another
terrace and then another 20 feet down to a second with a small swimming
pool and then yet another terrace which is his truck garden. It is a real
gem. The gouse is full of beautiful Chinese furniture. George has a chauffeur
cook, gardener, coolie
and wash anah, quite an establishment and not the
least of the attractions.
We did not get home until late so had an early
snack (after George's enormous steak lunch) and to bed early. My cold is
better.
Thurs. Dec. 10t4h Shopping. One interesting government development in
Kowloon was the reclaiming of a large tract of tidal shallowa where a complex
of apartments surrounds a harbor and provides a perfect shelter for junks
and small boats during typhoons or rough weather.
We have fairly definite plans (for us) now.
We leave here at 1 p.n. on
Dec. 16 for Manila and leave there on the 20th for Honolulu arriving the
same day (thanks to gaining a day crossing the International Date line).
You will no doubt wonder about the Chinese Communists, and so do we.
Outwardly they and China might as well be five thousand miles away. The
bee hive which is Hong Kong goes on as though everyone expected to be here
forever.
The government has just finished a 1,000 bed hospital, a
mountain is being truncated to provide space for another apartment, thousands
of men work around the clock on new buildings, in factories and on docks.
The first time I was here after the Communist take-over in China the
Communist flag was everywhere.
The next time about five years later I saw
a few and this time none.
Real Estate prices in the heart of Kowloon or
Victoria (Hongkong) are higher than New York, something like 500 U.s. dollars
per square foot.
Friday Dec. 11
We had a trip by car all around this island with coffee
at the Repulse Bay Hotel where we lived for a while.
Then we had lunch
at the Peiving restaurant with C.H. (Patty Woo. Others there were Mr. and
Mrs. Bill Cowden, PAA#1, George Sellett and my old friend Nixon, former
Postal Commissioner at Canton.
We had all of our old favorites, Pekin
duck, sharks fin soup, mandarin fish, chicken and walnuts, bahboo shoots,

-4-
water chestnuts, etc.
Mr. Nixon was the man who made it possible for us to
validate the Canton-Shanghai route but thats a long story which I'll save
for another time.
Sat. Dec. 12th
George Sellett's chauffeur took us for a drive around Kowloon
and the whole of the so called "New Territory" which is the leased area.
It
was like the old days in China, after we got out of the "Concrete Jungle".
High mountains franing fertile valleys in which every foot of land is used.
Hakka women with their unique hats of wide flat straw fringed with black
cloth which hangs down all the way around five or six inches, plowing the
fields with water buffalo. They are descended from the aboriginal people
who were here when the Chins came down from the north.
Many of you have
read Michener's Hawaii and may remember that the heroine, Mrs. Kee, was a
"big foot Hakka". We drove out to a place where there was a road block and
a narrow strip of "no man's land" which separated the leased territory from
Communist China. A Hong Kong police tower on high ground keeps constant watah
that no Chinese from Red China get into the leased territory. However,
fugitives continue to dross the border to add to Hong Kong's problem of
where to put them and how to feed them.
which few drivers know how to make so we are again indebted to George Setlett.
It is all so fantastic, especially after a ride such as we had, this

Sunday Dec. 13th
We spent the morning shopping, most of the shops stay open
and all building activity goes on just like any other day in the week.
Will
wind this up now and perhaps write
once more before we get home.
We hope
this reaches you by Christmas.
It carries our best wishes for a very
Merry Christmas and Happy New Year for each and every one of you.
Harold
